g.text: Session semantics and pitfalls — retraction, collection, and keying
gap 40s forces retract 7 then emit 11 · ignoring the key turns 5 sessions into 2
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
THE RETRACTION CASE — key "b", gap 40s
the window was already reported when the event that belongs to it arrived
the session as first emitted (event 4)
id 7 arrives at event 7 (et 12:00:50)
within 40s of the session's start — it belongs
the session as it must now be
so the pipeline must publish
retract 7, then emit 11
Without the retraction a consumer that adds panes reads 18 for a session worth 11.
This is the ch02 accumulation question arriving with no choice attached: a session that changes shape MUST retract, because the old pane
described a window that no longer exists.
Step 1/4 — at gap 40s, a late event forces a RETRACTION
A session is the one windowing where the published thing can stop existing. At gap 40s the session [12:01:30, 12:01:30] ids 2 sum 7 is emitted at
event 4; then id 7 arrives and it becomes [12:00:50, 12:01:30] ids 7,2 sum 11 — a different window, with different bounds. The old pane is not
stale, it is about something that is no longer there.
Session semantics and pitfalls — retraction, collection, and keying
gap 40s forces retract 7 then emit 11 · ignoring the key turns 5 sessions into 2
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
WHEN EACH SESSION IS ACTUALLY DONE
a session ends at its last event; it is DONE at end + gap (120s) in watermark terms
event 4, when the watermark reaches 12:03:05
event 8, when the watermark reaches 12:08:00
NEVER — watermark never reaches 12:11:00
event 8, when the watermark reaches 12:08:00
event 8, when the watermark reaches 12:08:00
A session that has been silent for 120s of WALL CLOCK may still grow — only the watermark passing end + gap rules that out.
And one session here is never collected at all, because the watermark never reaches 12:11:00. Its state is held for the life of the job.
Step 2/4 — sessions are collected by the WATERMARK, not by looking idle
"Looks idle" and "is done" are different claims, and only the second one lets you free memory. Each row's right-hand column is a watermark event,
not an elapsed time — and the last row shows the case that costs: a session nothing ever collects, holding its state until the pipeline stops.
Session semantics and pitfalls — retraction, collection, and keying
gap 40s forces retract 7 then emit 11 · ignoring the key turns 5 sessions into 2
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
THE GAP IS MEASURED WITHIN A KEY
an event that would have merged, if the key were ignored
key "b" session 1 ends at
key "b" session 2 starts at
12:03:40 — a silence of 130s, more than the 120s gap
id 3 (key "a") has et
12:02:10 — only 40s after session 1 ended
does it join key "b"'s session?
NO — different key, so the gap never sees it
Ignore the key and the 5 keyed sessions collapse to 2, because events from different users fill in each other's silences.
id 3 is the concrete case: 40s after key "b" went quiet, well inside the gap — and correctly invisible to key "b".
Step 3/4 — sessions are per KEY — and the near miss proves it
This is why "sessions are keyed" is a correctness statement rather than an implementation note. id 3 sits 40s after key "b"'s first session ended,
well within the 120s gap — and it belongs to key "a", so it must not extend key "b". Drop the keying and 5 sessions become 2: users' activity
merges into one fictional visit.
Session semantics and pitfalls — retraction, collection, and keying
gap 40s forces retract 7 then emit 11 · ignoring the key turns 5 sessions into 2
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
MATCH THE SHAPE TO THE QUESTION
four questions, four shapes — and one that needs a definition first
"how many per 120s?"
fixed — 4 answers totalling 45
"what is the rolling 120s figure?"
sliding — 2x the output, totals not comparable to input
"how long was each visit?"
sessions — 3 for key a, 2 for key b, at gap 120s
"how many visits did this user have?"
unanswerable until the gap is stated: 4 / 3 / 2 / 1
Only the last row has no answer in the data. 4 at gap 40s, 3 at gap 120s, 2 at gap 130s, 1 at gap 300s — all correct, for different definitions
of a visit.
Choosing the window shape is therefore part of specifying the question, which is why it is not an implementation detail.
Step 4/4 — so the window shape IS part of the answer
The shape is chosen by reading the question, and the last row is the one that catches people out. "How many visits?" cannot be answered by any
amount of engineering until someone fixes the gap — key a has 4, 3, 2, 1 visits at 40s, 120s, 130s, 300s, and every one of those answers is right.
